 Advertisement Trump administration drops legal fight to overhaul student loan forgiveness program
 Advertisement Updated: 7:07 AM EDT Oct 22, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ By HEATHER HOLLINGSWORTH Trump administration drops legal fight to overhaul student loan forgiveness program
 Updated: 7:07 AM EDT Oct 22, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ By HEATHER HOLLINGSWORTH The Trump administration moved Wednesday to end its legal fight to overhaul a popular student loan forgiveness program. 
 The Department of Justice appealed after federal judges ruled in June in favor of advocates who said the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program risked becoming a tool for political retribution. But it dropped two appeals Wednesday in single-sentence joint agreements, which stipulated that each side would pay its own fees. 
 Advertisement Federal officials provided no explanation, but advocates praised the ruling. 
 Related video: Trump administration addresses health care price transparency 
 “The Trump administration’s attempt to weaponize public service loan forgiveness against organizations it disagrees with was anti-democratic and unlawful from the start,” Dan Zibel, an attorney for the group Student Defense, said in a written statement. “This is a significant victory for millions of Americans who have dedicated their careers to public service.”
 The PSLF program was designed to make jobs in government, public schools, fire and police departments, public hospitals and nonprofits more attractive by forgiving loans for qualified employees after a decade’s worth of payments. 
 But last fall, President Donald Trump’s administration wrote a new rule to empower Education Secretary Linda McMahon to kick employers out of the program if she decides their work has a “substantial illegal purpose.” 
 The vaguely phrased rule was targeted at employers who support undocumented immigrants or transgender youth, potentially affecting borrowers who worked at schools, public hospitals and legal aid groups. 
 The overhaul amounted to a major reworking of a program that has canceled loans for more than 1 million Americans. 
 But just before it was set to take effect in July, U.S. District Judge Myong Joun in Massachusetts vacated the U.S. Education Department’s changes, saying they overstepped the agency’s power and threatened to violate First Amendment protections for free speech. The ruling came in response to a pair of lawsuits filed by more than 20 states along with a coalition of nonprofit groups and cities. 
 On the same day, District Judge Amir Ali in Washington issued a similar ruling in a case brought by nonprofit organizations.
